关键词: University of Oregon's RAPID-EC Research Group
主要内容: A new Care.com survey indicates that the lack of school and child care options is pushing some parents out of the workforce. Over 73% of parents with children under 15 plan to make major changes to their professional lives due to the lack of child care. About 15% are considering leaving the workforce altogether. Deb Perelman, founder of Smitten Kitchen, warns that working parents may face "compassion fatigue" from workplaces as they continue to balance work and child care responsibilities. Nearly 66% of respondents reported that their productivity at work has suffered, and over 55% feel they are letting down their colleagues. About 65% of working parents start late or end their workday early to care for their children. The struggle to balance work and child care has impacted their ability to perform well at work, with 64% reporting at least one major work failure since the pandemic began. Only 15% of working parents receive employer-sponsored child-care benefits, highlighting the need for more support and resources. A June report from the University of Oregon's RAPID-EC Research Group also highlights the lack of child care and school options is pushing some parents out of the workforce. Nearly half, 47% of working families, have lost the child care they used before the pandemic. Of families using child-care centers, 60% reported losing their provider. Congress allocated $3.5 billion in emergency funding to child care in the CARES Act, helping 23 states offer grants to child-care providers. However, more than 40% of child-care centers remain closed in some states, and most report the funds are already gone. The House of Representatives passed a set of bills last week that would provide over $60 billion in direct funding to the child-care industry. Democrats are pushing to get these provisions included in the next comprehensive relief package, but the Republican-led legislation has only allocated $15 billion toward child care and $70 billion for K-12 schools. Experts say it will likely take actions by both the government and employers to ensure that there's no lasting effects on working parents as they continue to juggle work and child-care responsibilities. Parents are faced with tough decisions for the upcoming school year, as many operate without child-care benefits. Kate Delany, a New Jersey-based mother, is struggling to balance her work responsibilities with managing homeschooling for her 8- and 11-year-old kids. Her husband, a middle school teacher, is planning to go back full-time this fall, adding to the stress. Delany says she is unsure what the fall will look like for her family, as her kids want to go back to school, but she prefers remote learning.
